title: Thou art the man (2 Samuel 11–12)
hook: adultery, murder, and a prophet's story that makes the king see himself
carry: I have sinned against the Lord

segments.voice: Yesterday, David dancing before the ark with all his might. Your line was dance anyway. Today, the same king at his lowest.

It's the turn of the year, when kings go out to war. David sends his army and stays home. One afternoon he walks on the palace roof and sees a woman bathing. Bathsheba, Bethsabee in the Douay-Rheims, the wife of Uriah, one of his own soldiers, away at the front. David sends for her. He's the king; nobody refuses the king. She becomes pregnant. To hide it, David brings Uriah home, but the loyal soldier won't sleep in comfort while his comrades are in tents. So David writes a letter, has Uriah carry it himself, and it says: put him at the front, and pull back.
screen: `THE KING STAYS HOME FROM WAR.` → `A WOMAN SEEN FROM THE ROOF.` → `A LETTER CARRIED BY ITS VICTIM.`

segments.voice: Uriah dies. David marries Bathsheba. Then God sends the prophet Nathan, who doesn't accuse. He tells a story. Two men in one city. One rich, with flocks and herds. One poor, with one little ewe lamb, which, the Douay says, grew up with his children, ate from his plate, drank from his cup, slept in his arms, and "was unto him as a daughter." A traveler visits the rich man, who doesn't take from his own flocks. He takes the poor man's lamb and serves it for dinner. David is furious. The man who did this deserves to die! He'll pay it back four times over! And Nathan says four words: "Thou art the man." David could see the injustice clearly as long as it was somebody else. The parable gets past his defenses, then turns around. And David, who holds all the power in the room, doesn't kill the prophet or spin it. He says, "I have sinned against the Lord." Nathan answers: the Lord hath taken away thy sin. The consequences still come; the chapters ahead are full of grief in David's house. But Nathan's word stands. Tradition gives this moment a song. The Douay's Psalm fifty, the Miserere, has a heading that sets it here, when Nathan came to David. It begins: "Have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy." The Church prays it in the Liturgy of the Hours, and Catholics bring its spirit into confession: say it plainly, and hear the word of pardon.
screen: `NATHAN TELLS A STORY.` · `THE POOR MAN'S LITTLE EWE LAMB.` · `I HAVE SINNED AGAINST THE LORD.` · `THE MISERERE: HAVE MERCY ON ME.` · then, large: `THOU ART THE MAN.`

segments.voice: Think of who could be your Nathan, someone who'd tell you the truth to your face, and what pattern they might name that you spot in others and not in yourself. Sit with it without arguing. If you pray, say the Miserere's first words: have mercy on me, O God, according to thy great mercy.
Nathan. The prophet whose four words to King David turned a story about someone else into a mirror, and led the king to confess. Today's word.
Your line: I have sinned against the Lord. Said plainly, and answered with pardon. Day four hundred five, done.

howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 51 (50 in the Douay numbering), the Miserere, at Morning Prayer on Fridays in the Liturgy of the Hours, and some use it to prepare for the sacrament of confession.

fork.setup: you're King David. a prophet has just tricked you into condemning yourself, in front of your court. you're the king. what do you do?
options: explain that kings live by different rules.
admit it: I have sinned against the Lord.
fork.reveal: David confesses, and Nathan says the Lord has taken away his sin. the consequences still come, but the king's first move is honesty.

original.note: Hebrew: I have sinned. In the Hebrew, David's whole confession to Nathan is just two words.

trapdoor: what you thought: a scandal story about a king and a bathing woman.
what it means: power, adultery and murder, undone by a prophet's story that makes the king see himself, and a confession without excuses.
what a scholar hears: in Hebrew David's confession is two words, chatati la-YHWH; and Psalm 51's heading ties the Miserere to this very moment.

chat.says: Why did Nathan tell King David a story instead of just accusing him?
options: The story got past David's defenses, then turned: thou art the man.
David had ordered that no one could accuse the king directly.
Nathan was afraid, so he hoped David wouldn't notice it.
chat.meaning: David saw the injustice clearly while it was someone else's. Nathan's four words turned the story into a mirror, and David confessed.

Bathsheba.meaning: Uriah's wife, whom King David took

Uriah.meaning: a loyal soldier David sent to die at the front

Miserere.meaning: Latin: have mercy; Psalm fifty in the Douay

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'spring' made the Douay's 'turn of the year'; cut the ranking line 'what sets David apart from so many powerful men in history'; narrator's 'the forgiveness is real' now attributed to Nathan's word; 'prays it constantly' and 'many Catholics' softened; 'most powerful man in Israel' cut from the fork.

Bathsheba's part is told carefully: the text gives her no words before 11:5, and David holds the power ('nobody refuses the king' is interpretive). Confirm the Keeper is comfortable with this framing.
'Kings go forth to war' in spring: the Douay says 'at the return of the year'; 'spring' is a common gloss. Confirm.
Psalm 51 (Douay 50) at Friday Morning Prayer in the Liturgy of the Hours (four-week psalter): confirm.
David's confession is two Hebrew words (chatati la-YHWH); 'just two words' counts chatati plus the divine name. Confirm; could say 'two words in Hebrew'.
